desc:
Two nodes are cousins if they are on the same level but have different parents. Build a new tree with the same shape in which the value of every node is replaced by the sum of the original values of all its cousins (0 if it has none). The root has no cousins, and neither do its children, so they become 0.

Return the new tree in the same level-order encoding, with -1 kept at exactly the same positions as in the input.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [5, 4, 9, 1, 10, -1, 7] the third level is [1, 10, 7], where 1 and 10 share the parent 4. Node 1 has the single cousin 7, node 10 also has the cousin 7, and node 7 has the cousins 1 and 10. The answer is [0, 0, 0, 7, 7, -1, 11].
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: For a node, cousins = (all nodes on its level) minus (the node and its siblings).
So you need two kinds of sums: the total of each level, and for every parent the total of its children.
New value of a node = levelSum[depth] - childrenSum[parent]. The root has no parent and simply becomes 0.
editorial: Counting cousins directly would be quadratic on wide levels. Instead use subtraction: the cousins of a node are all nodes of its level except the ones that share its parent (the node itself and its sibling, if any). With the level total S[d] and the sum C[p] of the values of the children of parent p, the new value is S[d] - C[p].

Compute S and C in one pass over the array (parents precede children), then write the new values in a second pass. The input values are the original ones in both passes, so no cousin sum can contaminate another. Time O(n).
